title: A giant ghostly bird
caption: Part of the Vela supernova remnant, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Pink and orange filaments swirl across this picture, suggesting the ghostly shape of a giant bird: orange wings spread wide, a long pink body, and for an eye, one bright pinkish star. Countless stars are sprinkled all around. What we are seeing is one small patch of the Vela supernova remnant: the tangled debris of a massive star that exploded 11 000 years ago.

When massive stars reach the end of their lives, they explode as supernovae and hurl their outer layers into space. The blast drives shock waves through the surrounding gas, squeezing and reshaping it. That is what created this web of filaments, which still shine because of the energy the explosion released.

The constellation of Vela is visible without a telescope from the southern sky, but details like these are far beyond what the eye can pick out. This view is part of a huge, detailed mosaic made with the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in the Chilean desert.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was taken with the OmegaCAM camera on ESO's VLT Survey Telescope, through u, g, r and i filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
filters: 350 nm · Optical u (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
480 nm · Optical g (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
625 nm · Optical r (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
770 nm · Optical i (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
659 nm · Optical H-alpha (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
understand.eye: The caption notes that Vela's stars are visible to the naked eye, but these faint filaments only emerge in long telescope exposures.
